name: Central giant cell granuloma of the jaw

reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours (Odontogenic and Maxillofacial Bone Tumours) / Burket's Oral Medicine
clinicalPearls: A benign but sometimes locally aggressive intraosseous lesion, occurring more often in the mandible, frequently anterior to the molars and able to cross the midline
Typically affects patients under about 30 years, with a female predominance
Presents as a painless or painful expansile swelling, with a well-defined uni- or multilocular radiolucency on imaging
Histology shows multinucleated giant cells within a fibrous, vascular stroma with areas of haemorrhage and haemosiderin
The histology is indistinguishable from the brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism, so serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone must be checked
Lesions are categorised as non-aggressive or aggressive on the basis of size, growth rate, pain, root resorption, and cortical perforation
Similar giant-cell lesions occur in cherubism and in some genetic syndromes such as Noonan and neurofibromatosis, which should be considered when lesions are multiple
Management ranges from curettage or enucleation and intralesional corticosteroid to more extensive resection for aggressive lesions
reference.pathophysiology: The central giant cell granuloma is a benign proliferation within the jaw consisting of osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells dispersed in a cellular, vascularised fibrous stroma of spindle-shaped mononuclear cells, with foci of haemorrhage and haemosiderin. The mononuclear stromal cells are regarded as the proliferating component, recruiting and fusing to form the giant cells, which resorb bone and generate the expansile lytic lesion. Although its precise trigger is uncertain and it was once attributed to trauma or reactive repair, it is now considered a benign proliferative process; crucially, systemic hyperparathyroidism produces a histologically identical brown tumour that must be excluded biochemically.
additionalDifferentials: Odontogenic keratocyst and other odontogenic cysts
Cherubism, which is bilateral and familial
additionalInvestigations: Dental panoramic and cross-sectional imaging (CT or CBCT) to define extent and locularity
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone to exclude hyperparathyroidism
Renal function and vitamin D assessment where hyperparathyroidism is suspected
Evaluation for syndromic associations if lesions are multiple or bilateral
Baseline imaging for monitoring after treatment
redFlags: Biochemical evidence of hyperparathyroidism indicating a brown tumour rather than a primary jaw lesion
Rapid growth, pain, paraesthesia, cortical perforation, or root resorption indicating an aggressive lesion
Multiple or bilateral lesions suggesting cherubism or a syndrome
reference.prognosis: Most lesions are cured by thorough curettage or enucleation, although aggressive lesions and a proportion of others recur and may need repeated or more extensive treatment; the outlook is excellent once hyperparathyroidism has been excluded or treated.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude hyperparathyroidism, so a brown tumour is mistaken for a primary jaw lesion
Under-treating an aggressive lesion with simple curettage and risking recurrence
Not considering cherubism or a syndrome when lesions are multiple
Inadequate long-term follow-up to detect recurrence
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours (Odontogenic and Maxillofacial Bone Tumours)
management: Exclude and, if present, treat hyperparathyroidism first with serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone, since the identical brown tumour must be ruled out
Surgical curettage or enucleation as the mainstay for most lesions, with histopathological confirmation by prior biopsy
More extensive resection for aggressive or recurrent lesions, with reconstruction and preservation of adjacent teeth and vital structures

Non-surgical adjuncts for aggressive lesions to shrink them and avoid mutilating surgery, such as intralesional corticosteroid injection, calcitonin, or antiresorptive or anti-angiogenic agents including denosumab and interferon
Serial imaging surveillance for recurrence after treatment
Evaluation for syndromic association when lesions are multiple or bilateral
Oral and maxillofacial specialist multidisciplinary management
